findings.reason: The protected app source uses the exact generic local name index for the source-string position during output reconstruction. That name conceals the coordinate whose difference-array coverage is being consumed and violates the campaign's explicit naming standard. The inert candidate renames only that binding and its use to source_position; AST normalization proves there are no other changes, while both protected sources remain untouched.

With source_position, the candidate is concise, conventional, and interview-ready. Names such as terminal, trie, longest, start, farthest_end, difference, coverage, and bold_open expose trie matching, interval union, and tag-transition roles directly, and no generic local named index remains.

Trie walks from every source start visit exactly the dictionary prefixes present in the string and record the exclusive end of the farthest terminal match. Marking [start, farthest_end) in a difference array covers the union of all matches from that start; shorter nested matches need no separate mark because they are contained in the farthest interval. Prefix-summed coverage is positive exactly on characters belonging to at least one occurrence. Opening and closing tags only on zero-to-positive and positive-to-zero transitions therefore produces one pair around every maximal covered run, naturally merging overlaps and adjacent matches while preserving every source character.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 758, Python, and the native boldWords(words, s) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms that every appearance of every keyword must be bold, the returned tag sequence must be valid, and the least possible number of tag pairs must be used. It also confirms a nonempty lowercase source of length 1 through 500, zero through 50 lowercase keywords, and keyword lengths 1 through 10.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2065974107 are algorithmically identical: both build the same terminal-marked trie, track the same longest word length, walk from each start to the farthest terminal, apply the same difference updates, reconstruct coverage transitions, and close a final open tag. The candidate preserves that exact data flow and differs from the app source only by the semantic source_position rename; native wrapper and typing differences remain the only protected structural adaptations.

The unchanged three authored workloads grow both source length and dictionary size from 4 to 16 while keeping word length two, so trie construction plus bounded source walks grow linearly while trying every word at every start grows quadratically. The exact candidate passed all twelve visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent -0.00 and a 1.00x largest runtime ratio. An independent trie-plus-mask implementation also passed, with exponent -0.00 and a 0.82x largest ratio. A correct character-by-character word-at-every-start control matched every output but failed only performance with relative growth exponent +0.91, distinguishing O(p + nL) trie traversal from the O(nwL) alternative.

The Approach accurately derives shared-prefix matching, the longest-word traversal bound, farthest-match sufficiency, difference-array union, and tag emission at coverage transitions. Its O(p + nL) time and O(p + n) space claims match the candidate algorithm and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves the all-appearances requirement, valid minimum-tag result, maximal merging of overlapping and adjacent coverage, both source examples, the exact nested-tag rejection in Example 1, all four constraints, the equivalence Note for problem 616, and the source mask-boundary hint.

Authenticated live Premium evidence confirms exactly two examples in source order, an explanation only for Example 1, four constraints, one Note identifying equivalent problem 616, one hint, and no source visuals or tables. The modular Reference and every composed section are hash-bound by a verified source_fidelity.json against live statement content hash 5ee5d240faa3908bc24a20ce6d86fa25c3dc8e66e18e4a76705e07f54e0c17ce.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly two examples. Their exact keyword arrays, source strings, and tagged outputs remain first in source order, including the overlap that must use one tag pair and the single matching keyword.

All twelve ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. The former hidden final-character, separated-range, and nested-match checks were exposed without weakening their expected behavior.

Authored and generated checks cover source lengths 1 and 500, dictionary sizes 0 and 50, keyword lengths 1 and 10, a minimum one-character full match, an empty dictionary, and maximum-size lowercase inputs.

Material behavior covers overlapping, adjacent, repeated, nested, prefix, suffix, and separated occurrences; full and partial coverage; final tag closure; unmatched and empty dictionaries; duplicate keywords; longest-keyword matching; valid tag placement; and use of one pair around every maximal covered run.

Expected results were checked against an independent direct occurrence mask that marks every character of every keyword appearance and emits tags at mask transitions. The oracle, protected app source, immutable native Solution, and rename-only candidate agreed on all fifteen authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 10668 exhaustive binary-alphabet states, 5000 deterministic random legal inputs, and two maximum-boundary inputs.

The unchanged 4-, 8-, and 16-character dictionary-cross-product workloads remain hidden and performance-only in benchmark.json, span 4x, and make the correct word-at-every-start control fail only the scaling verdict.
